newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to sell reforms in Russia's second city.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to sell reforms in Russia's second city.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, embroiled in a fresh tussle with his communist opponents over Russia's future, will travel to St Petersburg on Friday to promote his new reform drive.
Yeltsin, who has thrived on a busy schedule since February after eight months of heart problems, will take time out from trying to speed up macro-economic reforms and map out a new foreign policy.
He will also make a surprising foray into high culture.

The president's visit to Russia's struggling second city, which includes a visit to a factory and talks with entrepreneurs and administrators, bears a striking resemblance to a meet-the-people tour last year ahead of his re-election.

The next poll is three years off and he cannot run again, but Yeltsin, concerned now about his historical legacy, is going out of his way to win the population over to the reformist burst which has accompanied his return to health.
An opinion poll published on Thursday showed that few Russians trusted their 66-year-old leader but many appreciated his latest efforts to put Russia's house in order.

Some analysts say that, with the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament resisting his tough new measures, Yeltsin may also be focusing on Russia's influential but struggling intelligentsia in case of a possible early parliamentary poll.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would sign a string of decrees in St Petersburg, home to some of Russia's greatest cultural treasures.
Some of them "will sound slightly unusual to Russian ears", Interfax news agency quoted Yastrzhembsky as saying, citing a possible decree "On St Petersburg as Russia's cultural capital".

Yeltsin will bring reform guru First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who launched his career in St Petersburg, and Economy Minister Yakov Urinson with him, hoping to jolt the former tsarist capital out of its provincial stagnation.
Consigned to second-rate status by the Bolsheviks, the city has failed since communism fell to live up to the vision of its 18th century founder Peter the Great as a "window on the West".
But it is now seeking to turn things around with a debut Eurobond to raise $300 million on international capital markets.
While his ministers seek ways to improve the city's image among investors, Yeltsin's first stop will be at a statue of Alexander Pushkin, where he will lay a wreath to Russia's most celebrated poet.
Yeltsin, a building engineer by training and not known for promoting the arts, will also chair a meeting of his Council on Culture and Art at the Russian Museum.

The museum, home to the biggest collection of Russian painting and, like all the arts, suffering from the cash squeeze which has accompanied Yeltsin's reforms, may get a cash pledge from the president in the tradition of his re-election drive.

NTV commercial television said in its weekly analytical programme Itogi on Sunday that while politicians and the intelligentsia had never been permanent allies in Russia, there were recent signs of a warming between the two groups.

"When the fate of the fatherland is being decided, the need arises for the authorities and the opposition to attract the conscience of the people to their side," it said, adding that the intelligentsia was thought to hold the key.
Yeltsin has huge powers in Russia, including to dissolve the lower house of parliament which is frustrating liberals in his government by stalling on spending cuts and a new tax code.

Itogi said the Duma was vulnerable to dissolution, adding: "It's quite possible that the authorities and the opposition, in reviewing their intellectual forces, are already guessing when and how it might take place."
